Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — student study guide written from this lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). There is no Aldughaither chapter for brain tumours. The Nov 2026 re-send of these slides is identical to this version (only the date changed).

Learning objectives

  • Classify common intracranial tumours according to their origin and biological behaviour.
  • Outline the initial clinical assessment and diagnostic work-up of a suspected intracranial tumour.
  • Describe the principles of managing raised ICP, seizures and other acute complications.
  • Explain the main treatment modalities — surgical resection, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and selected targeted/systemic therapies.

1. How we classify intracranial tumours

By originBy biological behaviourBy molecular profile
Primary (arising from brain, meninges, nerves or pituitary) vs secondary/metastatic (spread from a systemic cancer)WHO CNS grade 1–4 reflects histology plus markers — grade 1 = slow-growing, curable with resection; grade 4 = aggressive and infiltrativeThe 2021 WHO classification integrates markers — IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, MGMT methylation — alongside histology to guide prognosis and therapy
  • Molecular era: glioma classification now uses molecular profile + histology, not histology alone; together they guide diagnosis, prognosis and treatment.

Common primary tumours by cell of origin

OriginExamplesTypical behaviour
GlialAstrocytoma, glioblastoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymomaGrade 1–4; glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain tumour
MeningealMeningiomaUsually grade 1, slow-growing, extra-axial, often resectable
Nerve sheathSchwannoma (e.g. vestibular schwannoma)Benign, slow-growing, arises from cranial/spinal nerve roots
EmbryonalMedulloblastomaHigh-grade, paediatric, posterior fossa, CSF-disseminating
Sellar regionPituitary adenoma, craniopharyngiomaUsually benign; morbidity from mass effect & endocrinopathy
LymphoidPrimary CNS lymphomaAggressive; treated primarily with chemotherapy ± radiotherapy
  • Notes add: ependymoma arises from the ventricular lining · schwannoma = well-defined focal lesion → candidate for stereotactic radiosurgery · embryonal tumours also include AT/RT (atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour), mainly paediatric · primary CNS lymphoma: biopsy, not resection (chemo-/radiosensitive).
  • The most common CNS tumours → meningioma, glioblastoma, pituitary adenoma, schwannoma. 438
  • Intra-axial heterogeneous enhancing lesion in the right premotor gyrus → high-grade primary brain tumour. 437 ×2

2. Metastatic disease & age/location patterns

  • Metastatic brain tumours are the most common intracranial tumour overall in adults — more frequent than any primary CNS tumour.
  • Common primaries: lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell, colorectal.
  • Classically multiple lesions at the grey–white matter junction.
  • Management depends heavily on the number of lesions and systemic disease control.
ChildrenAdults
LocationPredominantly infratentorial (midline)Predominantly supratentorial
ExamplesMedulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymomaGlioma, meningioma, metastasis, primary CNS lymphoma
Age clue (notes)Embryonal tumours are mainly paediatricOlder (≈ 50s–60s): think metastasis · younger (18–40): primary tumour such as glioma
  • Metastases can be solitary or oligometastatic; management depends on systemic stage/control, number of lesions, size and location, presentation/performance status.
  • Haemorrhage-prone metastases: melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, HCC (also lung, osteosarcoma). A brain metastasis presenting with haemorrhage → suspect one of these primaries.
  • 6-year-old, headache, vomiting, frequent falls, midline posterior fossa tumour → medulloblastoma, ependymoma, (pilocytic) astrocytoma. 439
  • Treated lung SCC, now headache, vomiting and left upper-limb weakness → MRI brain showing a right frontal lesion (metastasis; contralateral to the weakness — CT would not "show a left parietal lesion"). 439 ×2

3. Initial clinical assessment

HistoryExamination
Headache red flags: new, progressive, worse lying flat/with Valsalva, wakes from sleepFull neurological exam — mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar, gait
New-onset seizureFundoscopy for papilloedema
Progression and tempo of any focal deficitFormal visual-field testing
Cognitive/personality change reported by familyCognitive screening when indicated
Known systemic cancer (risk of metastasis)Vital signs — assess for Cushing triad
  • History themes: mass effect / raised ICP (headache, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision), seizure, progressive neurological symptoms; red flags — cognitive/personality change, known malignancy.
  • Cushing's triad = high systolic BP (wide pulse pressure), low HR, low/irregular RR. 432
  • Early-morning headache of raised ICP → increased systemic PCO₂. 434 ×2
  • 60-year-old, progressive left-sided weakness (arm > leg) over 3 months + left UMN facial palsy, normal speech → right frontal glioblastoma (progressive = tumour; sudden = stroke). 434 ×2
  • 10-year-old girl, headache + unstable gait, past-pointing and pendular reflexes → medulloblastoma of the cerebellum. 432 ×5
  • Seizure + enhancing lesion of the left inferior frontal lobe → difficulty in expression (Broca). 437

4. Imaging & adjunct studies

StudyRole
CT head (non-contrast ± contrast)First-line if acute presentation — confirms a mass, assesses haemorrhage, hydrocephalus and herniation risk
MRI brain with & without contrastDefinitive characterization and surgical planning; add advanced sequences (perfusion, spectroscopy) as needed
Endocrine labsFor sellar/parasellar lesions — full anterior pituitary panel ± visual fields before intervention
CSF studiesCytology if leptomeningeal spread or CNS lymphoma suspected — only after imaging excludes an LP contraindication (mass effect/herniation risk)
Systemic work-upCT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± tumour markers when a metastasis is suspected and no primary is known
  • Lumbar puncture is unsafe with mass effect/herniation risk — image first; CSF cytology only if imaging shows no contraindication.
The students' notes wrote "MRI without contrast"; the slide says MRI brain with & without contrast — contrast-enhanced MRI is the standard tumour protocol. Follow the slide.
  • Brain tumour suspected — the study to perform primarily → CT scan. 429 ×3
  • Headache, visual changes and bilateral milky nipple discharge → serum TSH and prolactin (sellar lesion → endocrine labs). 441

5. Getting a tissue diagnosis

  • Imaging suggests a diagnosis; histology (plus molecular testing) confirms it and drives adjuvant treatment.
ToolWhen / what
Stereotactic biopsyDeep, eloquent or multifocal lesions where resection carries high risk — tissue with minimal morbidity
Open resectionPreferred when safely achievable — diagnosis plus simultaneous therapeutic debulking/cytoreduction
Intra-operative frozen sectionRapid preliminary diagnosis in theatre to guide the extent of resection in real time
Molecular markersIDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, MGMT promoter methylation refine glioma diagnosis, prognosis and chemosensitivity
  • What surgery provides: tissue diagnosis · debulking/resection · relief of mass effect · treatment of life-threatening complications.
  • "We aim for resection in every tumour except primary CNS lymphoma" — highly chemo-/radiosensitive, so biopsy, not major resection.

6. Managing raised ICP

Medical measures

MeasureSlide
Head position & ventilationElevate the head of the bed to 30°; maintain normocapnia (avoid hypercapnia; brief hyperventilation only as a bridge in impending herniation)
OsmotherapyMannitol or hypertonic saline draw free water out of brain tissue and reduce ICP acutely
CorticosteroidsDexamethasone reduces vasogenic oedema around tumours (especially metastases) — not for cytotoxic oedema
Fluids & sedationAvoid hypotonic fluids and hypotension; adequate analgesia/sedation limits ICP surges
  • "You are the intern" — raised ICP: (1) ABC — secure the airway if consciousness falls, support breathing, stabilize circulation → (2) urgent CT brain once stabilized → (3) medical bridge: head up ≈ 30°, mannitol 1.5 g/kg, 3% saline, hyperventilation → (4) surgical: EVD, decompressive craniectomy, debulking, ICP monitor.
  • Notes' case: CT shows a left frontal tumour with massive haemorrhagic transformation, rupture into the ventricle and midline shift; theatre is busy → start the medical measures (head up, osmotherapy, hyperventilation, avoid agitation) before going to the OR. Know the doses for the OSCE. Hyperventilation target commonly PaCO₂ ≈ 30–35 mmHg. Avoid agitation (raises ICP).
Mannitol dose: the lecture gave 1.5 g/kg; most references quote 0.25–1 g/kg. For the exam, follow the doctor (1.5 g/kg) but recognise the book range.
  • Frontal tumour surrounded by massive brain oedema → dexamethasone (vasogenic oedema). 438 ×2
  • Most potent and fastest way to lower ICP → controlled hyperventilation (only briefly, as a bridge). 437
  • Treatment of raised ICP → head elevation (not flexion, lateral position or head-down). 429 ×2
  • Tumour patient collapses with high ICP — the pressure–volume curve → keyed "shifts to the right" (he is on the steep part: a small extra volume causes a large rise). 438

Surgical measures

MeasureWhen / why
External ventricular drain (EVD)Diverts CSF for obstructive hydrocephalus; also allows direct ICP monitoring and therapeutic drainage
Decompressive craniectomyRemoves a bone flap so swollen brain can expand — when medical measures fail or herniation is imminent (flap may be left off)
Emergent tumour debulkingWhen the tumour itself causes acute deterioration or herniation — diagnosis and treatment combined
Invasive ICP monitoringGuides therapy in critical care when the clinical exam is unreliable (e.g. sedated patient)

7. Seizure management

Established seizuresProphylaxis & emergencies
AEDs are started after a tumour-related seizure has occurredRoutine prophylactic AEDs are NOT recommended for patients who have never seized — reserved for those with a seizure history
Levetiracetam is commonly favoured — minimal drug interactions, available IVStatus epilepticus = medical emergency: secure airway, IV benzodiazepine first line, then a loading AED; involve critical care early
Choice individualized around interactions with chemotherapy/steroids and side effects
  • Seizure steps (notes): protect the airway (ABC) → terminate the seizure with a short-acting IV benzodiazepine → prevent recurrence by loading a longer-acting AED (e.g. phenytoin). A brain tumour alone, without a prior seizure, does not mean chronic AED therapy; peri-operative AED use depends on the circumstances.

8. Other emergencies to recognize

HydrocephalusIntratumoral haemorrhageHerniation syndromes
Obstructive (tumour blocking the CSF pathway) vs communicating (impaired CSF absorption) — both may need urgent CSF diversion (EVD)Certain tumours — metastatic melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma; high-grade glioma — bleed spontaneously → sudden deteriorationUncal (CN III palsy, contralateral hemiparesis), central (bilateral decline), tonsillar (respiratory arrest) — recognize early warning signs
  • Rule of thumb: acute deterioration in a tumour patient → think raised ICP/herniation, seizure, haemorrhage (or hydrocephalus).
  • Silent, then sudden: gliomas may grow very large and infiltrate deep structures before causing major symptoms — a patient may be walking and stable, then deteriorate abruptly from acute intratumoral bleeding.

9. Treatment — a multidisciplinary approach

  • Decisions are made by a tumour board — neurosurgery, neuro-oncology, radiation oncology, neuropathology and neuroradiology — weighing tumour biology against the patient's functional status and goals.
  • Modalities: surgery · radiotherapy · systemic therapy · rehabilitation · supportive & palliative care.

Surgical resection — goals & techniques

  • Goal: maximal SAFE resection — remove as much tumour as possible while preserving neurological function.
TechniqueUse
Extent of resectionGross total vs subtotal resection is a key prognostic factor, especially in glioma
Image-guided neuronavigationMRI-based intra-operative "GPS" for the tumour and adjacent eloquent structures
Awake craniotomyReal-time language/motor testing during resection near eloquent cortex
Intra-operative MRI & mappingConfirms extent of resection and functional boundaries during surgery (time-consuming)
Endoscopic approachesMinimally invasive corridor for sellar/skull-base tumours (e.g. endonasal transsphenoidal)
  • Core principle: maximum SAFE resection, not maximum resection — tumour in or near the motor cortex may limit resection. Intra-operative neuromonitoring also protects function.

Radiotherapy — types & indications

TypeIndication
Fractionated external-beam RT (EBRT)Standard adjuvant treatment for high-grade gliomas, daily fractions over several weeks to limit normal-tissue toxicity
Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) — Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, LINACSingle/few high-precision fractions for small lesions — metastases, meningiomas, vestibular schwannomas (not for diffuse glioma)
Whole-brain RT (WBRT)Multiple brain metastases or diffuse leptomeningeal disease, balanced against neurocognitive side effects (notes: lymphoma, small-cell malignancy)
Proton beam therapySharper dose fall-off spares tissue — paediatric and skull-base tumours (notes: e.g. chordoma)

Chemotherapy & targeted / systemic therapy

AgentUse
Temozolomide + radiotherapyStupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation followed by adjuvant temozolomide = standard of care for glioblastoma
Bevacizumab (Avastin)Anti-VEGF antibody for recurrent glioblastoma; also reduces vasogenic oedema and steroid dependence (notes: effect on survival limited/uncertain)
Targeted & immunotherapyBRAF inhibitors for BRAF-mutant tumours (notes: including selected craniopharyngiomas); immunotherapy/vaccines under investigation
Hormonal / medical therapyDopamine agonists (e.g. cabergoline) can shrink prolactinomas, often avoiding surgery altogether

10. Primary treatment by tumour type

TumourPrimary treatment approach
Low-grade gliomaMaximal safe resection ± observation or adjuvant RT/chemotherapy based on molecular risk
Glioblastoma (grade 4)Maximal safe resection → concurrent chemoradiation → adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp protocol)
MeningiomaObservation if small/asymptomatic; resection for symptomatic/growing lesions; SRS as an alternative or adjunct
Brain metastasis (single/oligo)Resection or SRS depending on size/location, plus consideration of WBRT and systemic therapy
Pituitary adenomaMedical therapy first for prolactinoma; endoscopic transsphenoidal resection for other functioning/mass-effect tumours
MedulloblastomaMaximal safe resection → craniospinal radiotherapy → adjuvant chemotherapy
  • Notes add: low-grade glioma — complete resection + favourable → surveillance; residual/high-risk → RT and/or chemo · meningioma — more common in women; headache alone does not prove the meningioma is the cause · metastasis — a radio-resistant metastasis may favour surgery · pituitary — large tumours, visual compromise, symptomatic non-functioning macroadenomas → usually surgery · medulloblastoma — post-op staging with brain + whole-spine MRI · primary CNS lymphoma → biopsy, not resection.
  • Pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm (visual loss + disturbed menses) → bitemporal hemianopia. 437 ×6

Key takeaways

  • Classify by origin (primary vs metastatic) and biological grade — frames prognosis and treatment intensity.
  • Assessment combines a focused history/exam with MRI and, when needed, tissue diagnosis.
  • Raised ICP, seizures, hydrocephalus and haemorrhage are the acute complications to anticipate and treat promptly.
  • Treatment is multidisciplinary: surgery, radiotherapy and systemic therapy are complementary, not competing.
  • The right combination — and sequence — depends on tumour type, location, and the patient in front of you.

Cases

Case 1 — glioblastoma: a management pathway

  • Presentation: progressive focal neurological symptoms; MRI obtained.
  • Imaging & work-up: MRI — a thick, irregular ring-enhancing mass with a necrotic centre and surrounding vasogenic oedema · started on dexamethasone for oedema; levetiracetam only if a seizure occurs · stereotactic biopsy confirms IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (WHO grade 4).
  • Management: maximal safe resection with intra-operative mapping (eloquent location) → concurrent chemoradiation → adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp) → ongoing MRI surveillance for recurrence.
Ring-enhancing lesion + necrosis in an adult → think high-grade glioma; treatment follows the Stupp protocol.

Case 2 — pituitary macroadenoma: choosing a pathway

  • Presentation: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, progressive bitemporal visual-field loss.
  • Imaging & work-up: MRI — sellar mass with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm · markedly elevated serum prolactin (prolactin-secreting adenoma) · formal visual fields confirm bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Management: first-line dopamine agonist (e.g. cabergoline) — often shrinks the tumour and restores vision medically · reserve endoscopic transsphenoidal resection for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy · serial prolactin and visual fields.
Not every sellar mass goes straight to surgery — a prolactinoma is treated medically first.

Additional imaging examples

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Classify by origin (primary vs secondary) and behaviour (grade 1–4; IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT for gliomas).
  • Metastases are the most common brain tumours overall. Older adults (≈ 50s–60s) → suspect metastasis; 18–40 → glioma more likely.
  • Children: infratentorial/midline (medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymoma). Adults: supratentorial.
  • Haemorrhage-prone metastases: melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, thyroid, HCC (also lung, osteosarcoma).
  • CT first in emergencies, MRI for detail. LP/CSF cytology only after imaging excludes mass effect or herniation risk.
  • Maximum SAFE resection, not maximum resection. Exception: primary CNS lymphoma → biopsy.
  • Acute deterioration: raised ICP/herniation, seizure, intratumoral haemorrhage, hydrocephalus.
  • Raised ICP bridge to OR: ABC → CT → head up ≈ 30°, mannitol 1.5 g/kg, 3% saline, hyperventilation. Surgical: EVD, decompressive craniectomy, debulking, ICP monitor.
  • Seizure: IV short-acting benzodiazepine, then load a longer-acting AED (phenytoin). A tumour alone does not mean chronic AEDs.
  • Match therapy to tumour: GBM = resection → RT + TMZ → adjuvant TMZ; prolactinoma = dopamine agonist; small asymptomatic meningioma = surveillance; SRS for focal lesions, not diffuse glioma.

References

  • Greenberg MS. Handbook of Neurosurgery, 9th ed. (2019) · Winn HR. Youmans and Winn Neurological Surgery, 8th ed. (2022) · Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of CNS Tumors (Neuro Oncol 2021) · Stupp R et al. Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma (NEJM 2005) · Weller M et al. EANO guidelines on diffuse gliomas (2021) · NCCN CNS Cancers guidelines · Vecht CJ et al. Seizure prognosis in brain tumors (Oncologist 2014).
